title: Phase 2 Pipeline Architecture and Plan
subtitle: XN task 1.4 section draft | Will Daly | October 20, 2026 (revised after all four 1.3 reports)
architecture: We propose a modular pipeline that preserves the relationship between a molecular drawing, its label, and any table needed to construct the complete molecule. This addresses the course project's central difficulty: scientific PDFs mix drawings with text, tables, and chemical notation (Northeastern University, College of Professional Studies, 2026). The proposed responsibilities in Figure 1 follow the team's planning issue and remain subject to member confirmation (XN Project Group 1, 2026a).

The front end produces page images and native PDF text in parallel, detects candidate regions, and applies a molecule filter. It retains page coordinates and table context. Readers then convert crops to candidate SMILES while preserving disagreements and abstentions. The proposed starting policy uses MolGlyph as the primary reader, keeps a SMILES with high confidence only when a second reader (MolScribe or MolSight) agrees with it, and takes MolSight's stereochemistry when MolSight and MolGlyph agree on the skeleton but differ on stereocentres. Label linking associates drawings with compound labels and table rows. Fully drawn molecules can proceed to export; scaffolds and substituents require R-group assembly. When evidence is ambiguous, the pipeline records an unresolved case rather than inventing a complete structure.

This design follows our evidence without assuming patent detection performance transfers to journal pages. The team table reports BioMiner at 73 of 220 unique internal molecules, with pooled precision of 67.6% and recall of 33.2%; the six-paper equal-weight values are 54.1% and 35.3%, respectively (XN Project Group 1, 2026c). No single reader run on the internal papers found more than 64 of the 220, because most molecules in papers 2, 4 and 19 are drawn as a scaffold with an R-group table. Assembly and context handling are therefore priorities, while detection and molecule discrimination still require evaluation on journal content. The reader policy rests on findings that held across members. MolGlyph was the most consistent reader on BioVista, Patent300, CLEF, UOB and JPO, and two members' independent MolGlyph setups got the same 790 of 1,000 shared BioVista crops right (Adranly, 2026; Daly, 2026). Its weak point is stereochemistry: MolNexTR led it on stereo-bearing USPTO structures (Adranly, 2026), and on 1,059 chiral BioVista crops where both read the skeleton correctly, MolSight alone had the stereochemistry right on 165 and MolGlyph alone on 95 (Jin, 2026). Requiring agreement between two readers raised internal-paper precision from 39% to 69% at a cost of 12 molecules (Daly, 2026). Neither reader's own confidence score separated right from wrong answers, so the policy relies on agreement instead (Adranly, 2026). These are baseline results, not results of the proposed pipeline.
plan: We propose file-based handoffs so readers with incompatible dependencies can run separately while sharing one evaluation environment. Phase 1 already needed this: MolNexTR runs on Python 3.8, MolSight needs newer packages than MolScribe, and DECIMER needs TensorFlow (Adranly, 2026; Chhetri, 2026; Jin, 2026). Each run preserves the PDF hash, package and model versions, configuration, hardware, and source revision. Page and region identifiers follow a molecule through recognition, label linking, and assembly. Coordinates stay in PDF points, with a stored transform between PDF points and page-image pixels. Intermediate records distinguish a rejected non-molecule, an abstention, and a processing error.

Peter's proposed module supplies pages, text, candidate crops, and raw table geometry. Bijay's supplies reader outputs and a documented consensus policy, starting from the agreement and stereochemistry rules above and testing whether MolNexTR or MolSight is the better second vote. Jin's links labels, scaffolds, and table rows using traceable evidence. Will's assembles scaffolds with text or image substituents and proposes maintaining the shared export adapter. The team must confirm the table-extraction boundary, reader disagreement policy, and export responsibility before implementation.

We propose reviewing the fields together by the October 25 interface target. Each member would contribute a module paragraph and a small input/output example, including one abstention or failure, by October 28. We will replace the smoke scaffold's stubs one at a time and test the handoffs before running the full chain. The proposed report schedule reserves October 30 for a complete draft and October 31 for comments, before the November 1 submission (XN Project Group 1, 2026b).

Evaluation will compare the existing reader baseline with added filtering, consensus, linking, and assembly. We will report per-paper and equal-weight precision and recall, pooled results, output counts, and rejected or unresolved cases. Salt, tautomer, and stereochemistry scoring rules remain unchanged, and R-group labels are scored by one convention: two members' 0% Markush results came from how R-groups were written (* versus [1*]), not from misread drawings (Adranly, 2026; Chhetri, 2026). Only 7 of the 222 internal answer rows have a stereocentre (Jin, 2026), so the stereochemistry rule is evaluated on BioVista's 2,056 chiral test crops rather than the internal papers. Because the six internal papers have already informed the design, they are a development benchmark; generalization claims require unseen papers, especially since reader rankings reversed between public datasets (Adranly, 2026). Cross-page tables, ambiguous attachment points, absent PDF text, and incompatible reader environments are the main integration risks.
